https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/ukraine-w.text: Warren Murray and agencies Updated Mon, August 10, 2026 at 1:19 AM UTC 0 Kim Jong-un, the North Korean dictator, with returned casualties in wheelchairs after he sent them to fight Ukrainian troops in Russia’s Kursk region.Photograph: KCNA via KNS/AFP/Getty Images Up to 50,000 North Korean soldiers will be deployed in Russia , Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, while calling on South Korea to provide support for Ukraine’s air defence. It is an increase from the estimated 30,000 announced by the Ukrainian president in July. Kyiv had found some North Korean missiles in Ukraine’s territory, he said. “It is absolutely clear that ⁠North Korea will continue to build its experience in modern warfare, receive licences from Russia, and receive all ​kinds of military tools from them.” This month, an official at Ukraine’s military intelligence told Reuters that a North Korean missile unit has begun deploying personnel and equipment to western Russia and the unit could be equipped with 120 ballistic ⁠missiles and six launchers for strikes against Ukraine. North Korea sent an estimated 14,000 soldiers to Russia’s Kursk region in 2024, helping Moscow fight an invasion by Ukrainian forces. Thousands have been wounded or killed . North Korea has supplied ​Russia with millions ‌of artillery and mortar rounds – sometimes of dangerously low quality, according to Russian milbloggers and troops – ​as well as ballistic missiles, long-range ​artillery and multiple-launch rocket systems, according to Ukrainian and independent assessments. Zelenskyy continued that Ukraine “would very much like to receive support from South Korea in ‌an area where we have a shortage”, referring to air defence systems . “We are ready to work on the drone deal and other areas as well,” he said, adding that Ukrainian diplomats “are in contact” with Seoul to push potential deals. Ukraine is very short of high-end ​air defences and Russia has ​tried to exploit this by using ​more ballistic missiles, which are very hard to shoot down without interceptors like the US-owned Patriot. Seventy Atacms short-range ballistic missiles are part of a weapons package that Ukraine is poised to buy from Turkey , according to US congressional documents (pdf) . The US would have to approve the resale of the American-origin weapons. The state department indicated to Congress it is prepared to give permission. Along with the M39 Atacms missiles, Turkey also plans to sell Kyiv 47,000 artillery rounds, 12 M270 multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS) and more than 2,000 cluster bombs, according to the notice from the US state department. Russian missiles struck a high-rise apartment block in the Saltivskyi district of Kharkiv, killing two people and injuring 13 , said regional head Oleh Syniehubov. Zelenskyy said eight people were wounded in Odesa, where strikes damaged the power grid, the port and residential buildings. He condemned an “absolutely brutal” strike targeting energy infrastructure near a shopping centre in Pavlohrad, Dnipropetrovsk region , that wounded nine people including four children. Russia said Ukrainian drones killed five people and injured two dozen others in the Belgorod region. Zelenskyy, in his evening address on Sunday, defended Ukraine’s replies to Russia’s attacks – including strikes on Russian oil refineries, air defence systems and radar stations – as “truly just responses”. “The Russian war will be increasingly felt at home, in Russia,” he said. The World Health Organization chief, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said a WHO warehouse stocking medical supplies in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro was destroyed in strikes on Friday. “I cannot say loudly enough: attacks on health care must stop. Otherwise, people are deprived of lifesaving healthcare,” Tedros posted. “Even wars have rules. One of those is that health must be protected!” Ukrainian drone strikes damaged commercial sites and a home in the Russian city of Novorossiysk, said the mayor, Andrey Kravchenko. A major fuel terminal is located at Novorossiysk that links Kazakhstan’s oilfields to markets around the world. It has previously been a target for Ukrainian strikes. Bulgaria summoned Ukraine’s ambassador after a drone entered Bulgarian airspace , the country’s public broadcaster BNT reported on Sunday. The drone exploded on Saturday close to an international gas pipeline shortly after crossing the border from Romania, the Bulgarians said. No casualties or damage were reported. Bulgaria’s defence ministry said the incident was likely accidental and involved a drone that appeared to be a Ukrainian type. Kyiv’s foreign ministry said Ukraine did not deliberately target Bulgaria and the two sides were in “close contact” about it. A “powerful explosion” believed to be from a combat drone was reported in the village of Crocmaz, in south-east Moldova near the border with Ukraine, local police said on Sunday. No one was injured by the impact, which caused a vegetation fire in the Stefan Voda district, police said, adding that “fragments of a combat drone were found at the scene” and would be examined by specialists. Police did not specify the origin of the drone. The UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, has urged allies to boost Ukraine’s air defences ahead of a winter that Vladimir Putin will seek to use as a “weapon” against Kyiv. Writing in the Sunday Times, Streeting warned that while Putin was currently losing the war, “Ukrainians know what winter brings, and how it can change the picture”. Allies’ efforts to assist Ukraine “must include greater resources for air defence”. “My task – alongside my German counterpart Boris Pistorius, with whom I co-chair the Ukraine defence contact group – is to turn the goodwill of some 50 nations into concrete help.” Pope Leo on Sunday said innocent people were being ⁠killed and wounded in Ukraine and Russia, and called for an end to ⁠the conflict. “Tragic incidents ⁠are ​multiplying, causing an ever-growing number of civilian victims, including children,” the pontiff said before worshippers ⁠gathered for Sunday’s Angelus prayer. “I renew my heartfelt appeal for international humanitarian law to be ⁠respected and for attacks against civilian targets to cease on ​both sides.” More than ‌16,000 civilians have been killed, according to the UN, the overwhelming majority of them Ukrainian . https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text: Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries’ meeting with Jared Kushner, the president’s influential son-in-law, has sparked backlash from his own party and other Donald Trump critics. The reported meeting comes months ahead of the November midterm elections in which Democrats are favored to retake the US House, a development that would make Jeffries speaker. If they are in the majority, Democrats are expected to use their oversight power to aggressively investigate the Trump administration, including self-enrichment by the president and his family. There are longstanding conflict-of-interest concerns about the way Kushner has continued to make money from foreign nations as he works on foreign affairs, including conflicts in Ukraine, Iran and Gaza. Asked about the reported meeting, Jeffries said in a statement: Throughout this Congress, Republicans have adopted a my-way-or-the-highway approach to governing that has failed the American people.

https://www.israelnationalnews.com/news/.text: REYKJAVÍK - I came to Iceland in love with Iceland. I leave heartbroken by it. For nearly two weeks my family and I traveled through what is unquestionably one of God’s great masterpieces. We drove beneath mountains disappearing into clouds, stood before thundering waterfalls, crossed black volcanic landscapes, watched glaciers descend toward the sea and experienced the surreal beauty of an island perched between Europe and America. Iceland is magnificent. But there was another Iceland that emerged during our visit - an Iceland I could never have imagined when I arrived. Again and again, I was recognized as “Rabbi Shmuley," the celebrity Jew and rabbi who is an outspoken supporter of Israel and confronted with hostility. I was cursed. I was continuously and repeatedly called “baby killer." “Free Palestine" was hurled at me incessantly - not as a political slogan at a demonstration, but directly at me, a Jewish man walking down a street with his Jewish family and IDF hero children who had come to get away from the war for Israel’s survival for just a few days. Related articles: Why is Mark Ruffalo using the genocide libel again? Sweden’s betrayal of Raoul Wallenberg Caitlyn Jenner supports Rabbi Shmuley Boteach The batons of Barcelona and the double standard against Israel I was told, in various formulations, that Zionists were not wanted in Iceland. I heard nonstop “F--- Israel." I was followed everywhere I went in the larger cities and verbally abused. I was confronted by strangers who seemed to regard the mere presence of a proud Jew and lover of Israel as a provocation. I was physically assaulted. Then I was assaulted a second time. And during one approximately 30-minute walk through Reykjavík, I counted seven separate hostile confrontations. Seven. Thirty minutes. I have documented this extraordinary experience across my Instagram and Facebook accounts so that people don’t have to take my word for it. The videos are there and have been watched my tens of millions of people worldwide. They went viral especially in Iceland. The faces are there. The confrontations are there. One of my posts documented what I described as my second assault in Iceland. Another recorded a verbal confrontation. Another showed an Icelandic couple confronting me on the street, with “F--- Israel" at the center of the exchange. Yet another captured a longer discussion with an Icelander over the supposedly convenient distinction between hating Israel and hating Jews. This wasn’t one unpleasant encounter. It became a pattern. And after enough encounters, a tourist ceases asking, “What is wrong with that individual?" and begins asking, “What is happening in this country?" Seven hostile confrontations in one 30-minute walk through Reykjavík. At what point do isolated incidents become an atmosphere? One of the most disturbing incidents came in a bar. I wanted to buy a beer. That’s it. Not deliver a lecture about Gaza. Not debate Icelandic foreign policy. Not ask why in ten days we had only seen five black people in a country that dares preach to Israel about tolerance. Not lead a pro-Israel demonstration. I wanted a beer. I was recognized, another confrontation ensued, and I was physically assaulted. Imagine traveling thousands of miles with your family to one of the world’s most celebrated tourist destinations and discovering that even buying a drink can become dangerous because someone recognizes you as a prominent Jewish defender of Israel. Afterward there was the predictable chorus: perhaps I provoke people by responding. Perhaps I should ignore them. Perhaps a public Jew should learn to walk away. Forgive me. Since when did the victim of harassment acquire the responsibility to disappear? A Jew should not have to remove his yarmulke, hide his Magen David, conceal his identity or remain silent in the face of abuse in order to purchase a beer safely in a European capital. And after repeated confrontations, I experienced something far more consequential than anger. Fear. There were moments during this trip when I genuinely feared for my physical safety and even for my life and the safety of my family. I have confronted antisemites throughout the world. I have been threatened before. I have been attacked before. I know that political disagreement can become heated without becoming dangerous. This was different because it was so incessant, so pervasive, so universal. And then the street hatred met the online hatred. Unhinged antisemite Candace Owens’ relentless obsession with Israel and attacks on me need little introduction. One of the posts I sent out during the trip described an attempt by Owens to publicize my family’s presence and inflame hostility while we were already being confronted in Iceland. Candace Owens jumped into the fray from the United States and demanded that “Viking Power" evict us from Iceland. You begin looking over your shoulder. You notice who is watching you. Your family notices. A pleasant walk stops being a pleasant walk because you wonder whether the next person who recognizes you will say hello, scream “baby killer," or put his hands on you. That is no way for any tourist to experience Iceland. And it is certainly no way for a Jew to experience Europe in 2026. I should not have to hide my yarmulke, conceal my Magen David, or surrender my voice in order to buy a beer safely in a European capital. My social-media pages became a running diary of this ugliness. Eye on Palestine, with 14 million followers. Openly called repeatedly for my assassination on Instagram. This is the frightening ecology of modern antisemitism. Someone recognizes a Jew. The confrontation is filmed. The video goes viral. Thousands cheer the person confronting the Jew. Influencers amplify the hostility. And the next person who sees the Jew in the street believes he too has permission to confront him. The digital mob becomes the physical mob. All the while we are told: This isn’t antisemitism. It is only anti-Zionism. Really? Then explain something to me. Why was the target an American rabbi? I am not a member of Israel’s government. I do not command the IDF. I do not determine Israeli military policy. I was walking through Iceland with my family. Yet strangers felt entitled to make me answer personally for Gaza because I am publicly Jewish and publicly, now and forever, stand with Israel. When people scream “Zionist" at a visibly Orthodox Jew as an epithet, “Zionist" is no longer functioning as a political description. It has become a socially acceptable substitute for another word. Jew. Of course, not every critic of Israel is an antisemite. Criticism of Israel is no more inherently antisemitic than criticism of France is anti-French. But there comes a point where intellectual dishonesty becomes absurd. If you see an Orthodox Jewish tourist and begin shouting at him about Israel; if you call him a “baby killer"; if you tell him Zionists are unwelcome; if you curse the Jewish state in his face and scream “F--k Israel" at the top of your lungs - and then insist that none of this has anything to do with Jews, you cannot seriously expect the Jewish victim to applaud the sophistication of your distinction. “When ‘Zionist’ becomes the epithet screamed at the Jew standing in front of you, it is fair to ask whether ‘Zionist’ has simply become Europe’s respectable substitute for ‘Jew.’" And what makes Iceland’s descent so painful is how different the country appeared only recently. From 2003 to 2016, Iceland’s First Lady was Dorrit Moussaieff, an Israeli-born Jew from Jerusalem, wife of President Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson. She became an Icelandic citizen and one of the country’s best-known public personalities. Contemporary Icelandic reporting described her unmistakably as Iceland’s First Lady. Think about that extraordinary contrast. Just over a decade ago, an Israeli-born Jewish woman from Jerusalem occupied Iceland’s most prominent ceremonial role alongside its president. Now an American Orthodox rabbi walks through Reykjavík and is repeatedly denounced over Israel. What happened? There were warning signs. In 2018, members of Iceland’s parliament seriously considered legislation prohibiting the non-medical circumcision of boys. For most Icelanders, circumcision may appear an obscure ritual. For Jews, brit milah is the covenant of Abraham, practiced for thousands of years and foundational to Jewish religious identity. The proposed legislation was real enough that Iceland’s own parliamentary records contain extensive submissions both supporting and opposing it. The Council of Jewish Communities of Latvia warned Alþingi that banning circumcision would effectively prohibit Jewish existence in Iceland. The proposed punishment was extraordinary: reports at the time said anyone performing such a circumcision could face up to six years in prison. The bill ultimately died. Thank God. But Jews noticed that in a European democracy in the twenty-first century it became seriously conceivable that a rabbi performing Abraham’s covenant could face years behind bars. Europe repeatedly tells Jews: We love Judaism. Then come the qualifications. We love Judaism without circumcision. We love Judaism without Israel. We love Jews provided their Jewishness never inconveniences the prevailing ideology. That is not tolerance. That is conditional acceptance. Icelanders will respond that their country has demonstrated genuine compassion toward Palestinians. That’s garbage. In 2008, Iceland accepted - get ready- 29 (!) Palestinian Arab refugee women and children who had been stranded in a desert camp on the Iraq-Syria border. UNHCR reported that the group consisted of eight families headed by women, several of whom had lost husbands in the Iraq conflict Saving refugees is noble. But 29? Seriously? In a country of only 350,000 people that is ninety percent empty? No. This was never about Palestinian Arab rights or Iceland would have tie in at least 10,000 refugees from Gaza, that was destroyed because of Hamas, the way countries take in refugees. This is all about hatred of Israel, in other words, antisemitism. Why should compassion for Palestinians require hostility toward Jews? Why must sympathy for one people become contempt for another? During our travels, my family and I were struck by how racially homogeneous much of Iceland appeared to us. We commented repeatedly on how few Black people we personally encountered during nearly two weeks traveling around the country. That is, of course, an anecdotal observation rather than a demographic study, and I would not pretend otherwise. Nor would it be accurate to claim Iceland accepts “no one." It has accepted refugees and has significant immigration. But precisely because Iceland wishes to present itself to the world as enlightened, humanitarian and tolerant, its moral test is not merely which distant populations it champions. The test is also how human beings standing on an Icelandic street are treated. Humanitarianism is cheap when its beneficiaries are abstractions. It becomes real when a person you disagree with is three feet in front of you. You cannot proclaim Palestinian Arab dignity while denying Jewish dignity. You cannot campaign against racism while intimidating Jews. And you cannot chant about human rights while making a Jewish tourist fear for his physical safety. There was something else I encountered in Iceland: a startling strain of anti-Americanism. Not disagreement with American policy. Something more visceral. Much of Europe despises Donald Trump. Icelanders may criticize President Trump every waking hour if they wish. Americans ourselves fight fiercely over our presidents. But Trump hatred does not justify hatred of Americans. Some of the hostility I experienced seemed part of a broader ideological package in which America is regarded as imperialist, Israel as colonialist, and an outspoken American Jew who supports Israel becomes a convenient symbol of both. That worldview is as simplistic as it is poisonous. America has been central to Europe’s security for generations. Iceland itself is a NATO ally. Political disagreement between democracies is healthy. Contempt for entire peoples is not. Then there is a practical reality Iceland ignores at its peril. Tourism is not some marginal Icelandic industry. It is fundamental to the country’s prosperity. According to Statistics Iceland, tourism directly accounted for 8.8% of Iceland’s GDP in 2025, up from 8.2% the year before. Nearly one dollar in every eleven generated in Iceland’s economy is therefore directly connected to tourism. Iceland’s entire global brand is based on a promise. Come here. See something extraordinary. Experience one of the safest, friendliest, most beautiful places on earth. But safety and hospitality are part of the product. Americans have choices. Jews have choices. Israelis have choices. Families deciding where to spend thousands of dollars on a vacation have choices. And nobody wants to travel across an ocean to be told that people like them are unwelcome. Iceland’s waterfalls are magnificent. Its glaciers are breathtaking. But no waterfall is beautiful enough to compensate for fearing that the next stranger who recognizes you may threaten or assault you. I do not want Jews to boycott Iceland. I want Iceland to change. That distinction is important. I have seen too much beauty here to wish this country ill. And I have visited probably five or six times and lectured to the Jewish community, tiny as it is, on every occasion. I met good Icelanders. Many were gracious and welcoming. It would be morally wrong for me to condemn an entire nation because of people who abused me, just as it is morally wrong for them to condemn every Jew because they despise Israel’s government. But neither will I sanitize what happened. Too often Jews are told not to make a fuss. Don’t call it antisemitism. Don’t embarrass anyone. Don’t exaggerate. Don’t answer back. Don’t make people uncomfortable. For two thousand years Jews have been advised to survive hostility by becoming less visible. I reject that advice. I am a Jew. I am a rabbi. I am a lover of Israel. And none of these things deprives me of my right to walk safely down a street in Reykjavík. I increasingly worry that Iceland is following the path of Ireland, where hostility toward Israel has become so culturally pervasive that the Jewish state is often discussed not as an imperfect democracy capable of terrible mistakes, but as something uniquely sinister and illegitimate. I am not going to manufacture a statistical claim that Iceland and Ireland are literally the two “most antisemitic" nations in Europe when reliable comparative evidence does not establish that ranking. I don’t need to. My firsthand experience is damning enough. On this trip I was cursed.I was verbally harassed repeatedly. I was called a baby killer. I was told Zionists were not wanted. I was physically assaulted. I experienced seven hostile confrontations in approximately 30 minutes in Reykjavík. My social-media accounts became a daily chronicle of abuse. And as I prepared to depart, I recorded my sadness that a country of such extraordinary grandeur and majesty could have become, in my experience, so consumed by hostility toward Israel and Jews who defend it. That departure reflection too is publicly documented. This happened in Iceland. In 2026. And that should trouble every decent Icelander far more than anything I have written in this column. I refuse to condemn an entire nation because some Icelanders hated me. But I also refuse to pretend that what happened to me did not happen. Iceland, what happened to you? How did the country that embraced a Jerusalem-born Jewish First Lady become a place where I experienced this degree of hostility as a Jewish visitor? https://www.politico.eu/article/turning-.text: Berlin’s political establishment is staggering after the far-right Alternative for Germany scored a historic victory in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday night, forcing mainstream parties to confront how to keep it from power — and explain its stunning rise. The AfD won 43.8 percent of Sunday’s vote, more than doubling its 2021 result. Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union crashed to 17.2 percent, its worst-ever showing in the eastern state. Thorsten Frei, leader of the CDU/CSU group in the Bundestag, called the result a “turning point for our country” and said conservatives must ask why they were no longer reaching voters. CDU Secretary-General Franziska Hoppermann rejected any debate over Merz’s future and again ruled out cooperation with either the AfD or The Left. Advertisement Advertisement Saxony-Anhalt’s incumbent premier Sven Schulze, from the CDU, struck a more sober note on Sunday night. “Some say this is a dark day for Saxony-Anhalt. I say: That’s democracy,” he told ARD. “The people went to the polls today.” The rout piles pressure on Merz, who once vowed to cut the AfD in half but has been chancellor while the far-right party has boomed in the polls. Social Democratic Party co-leader Lars Klingbeil called the vote a “signal to Berlin” and said the result should prompt the federal government to reflect on its policies. Co-leader Bärbel Bas said the result was “frightening many people,” while Green co-chair Felix Banaszak described the AfD surge as “dramatic.” The Left’s Heidi Reichinnek branded the result “catastrophic,” blaming federal government policies for creating fertile ground for the far right. But the CDU’s refusal to cooperate with The Left makes constructing an anti-AfD majority harder. Left-populist BSW founder Sahra Wagenknecht declared the “firewall policy” a failure in a post on X, warning another coalition built purely to exclude the AfD would be an “affront” to voters. The AfD, meanwhile, claimed a mandate to govern. Co-leader Alice Weidel hailed a “historic result,” while fellow co-leader Tino Chrupalla declared: “Ulrich Siegmund will be our new minister-president,” referring to the party’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt. Advertisement Advertisement Chrupalla then turned Merz’s own rhetoric back on him: “We’ve cut the CDU in half.” Yet the AfD won just 39 of 83 seats in Saxony-Anhalt, leaving it just short of a majority. The far right’s rivals now face a scramble to find a government capable of surviving without it. Chrupalla, meanwhile, said the party would send invitations for talks to all other parties. “Then we’ll see who slaps away our hand,” he told public broadcaster ARD on Monday. Asked whether the AfD could push for fresh elections if no workable majority emerges, Chrupalla said the party was “prepared for all scenarios.”
